title: Major fires in Indonesian Borneo are possible under all ENSO phases
abstract: Abstract Major fires in Indonesian Borneo over the past few decades caused devastating impacts on human health, livelihoods, economy, the natural habitat and the carbon sink. Despite the proven link between the positive phase of the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and rainfall deficit, a primary driver of fires, the rare occurrence of historical major fires makes it difficult to robustly assess their climatic cause using purely the observational record. We analysed a large initialised ensemble of global climate simulations to demonstrate that although the risk of severe fires that level or surpass those observed in 1997 and 2015 is strongly boosted by an El Niño by a factor of 2.7, such risk exists regardless of the ENSO phase. Other factors modulating the risk include the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) and a Rossby wave train over the southern extratropics which acts to decouple the rainfall response from the ENSO state. Our study highlights that even in places characterised by high seasonal predictability, there is still a possibility of high impact weather events to occur against the expected response to a given teleconnection mode, which implies the necessity to build long-term resilience against the associated hazards on top of improving our sub-seasonal forecasting capability.
problem: The rarity of major historical fires in Indonesian Borneo makes it difficult to robustly assess their climatic causes and true risk under different climate conditions using solely the limited observational record.
method: The paper analyzes a large initialised ensemble of global climate simulations using statistical methods to robustly assess the climatic drivers of rare major fires in Indonesian Borneo, overcoming the limitations of the short observational record and revealing risks that exist even without an El Niño event.
task: The task is to assess the climatic drivers of major fires in Indonesian Borneo by analyzing a large ensemble of global climate simulations to overcome the limitations of the sparse observational record of these rare events.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: We used the Canadian Fire Weather Index (FWI) to estimate fire risk in the study region. Based on these inputs, the moisture content in organic matter is evaluated, represented by Drought Code, Duff Moisture Code and Fine Fuel Moisture Code...We computed the daily FWI using the meteorological inputs from GloSea6 on its native grid and obtained the area average within the study region.
